payload.stem: Two frictionless ramps rise to the same height of $0.8\text{ m}$. Ramp 1 is $3\text{ m}$ long and ramp 2 is $5\text{ m}$ long. options.text: Both blocks have the same speed of $3.96\text{ m/s}$, because each block loses the same gravitational potential energy $mgh$ and gains the same kinetic energy.
options.why: With no friction, $mgh=\tfrac12mv^2$ on either ramp, so $v=\sqrt{2gh}$, which does not depend on the length of the ramp.

options.text: Both blocks have the same speed of $2.8\text{ m/s}$, because the kinetic energy is $mgh$ and equals $mv^2$.

options.text: The block on ramp 1 is faster, because it has the greater acceleration and so the greater final speed.
options.why: A greater acceleration over a shorter distance gives the same speed, since $v^2=2aL$ with $a=gh/L$ gives $v^2=2gh$ for both.

options.text: The block on ramp 2 is faster, because it travels the greater distance and so gains more speed.
options.why: Overlooks the smaller acceleration on the longer ramp; the speed depends on the height only.

options.why: Confuses a constant flow rate with a constant speed, ignoring the change in the cross-sectional area.

misconceptions.description: Leaves out the factor $2\pi$ in the period.
Uses only the mass of the block that was originally attached and leaves out the added mass.

payload.explanation_en:
The correct answer is $2\pi\sqrt{\frac{m+M}{k}}$. The mass that oscillates is $m+M$ and the restoring force constant is $k$, so $T=2\pi\sqrt{(m+M)/k}$.
$\sqrt{\frac{m+M}{k}}$ is incorrect: Leaves out the factor $2\pi$ in the period.
$2\pi\sqrt{\frac{m}{k}}$ is incorrect: Uses only the mass of the block that was originally attached and leaves out the added mass.
$2\pi\left(\sqrt{\frac{m}{k}}+\sqrt{\frac{M}{k}}\right)$ is incorrect: Adds the masses outside the square root.

key_scoring.notes: T = 2π√((m+M)/k) is the unique correct option. The stem states an ideal spring and a frictionless surface, and the stuck-together blocks move as one mass.

stimulus_expression.notes: No stimulus is needed. The wording is clear and the options are short parallel expressions.

distractor_explanation.notes: The distractors encode distinct misconceptions: missing 2π, ignoring the added mass, and adding the square roots. The explanation covers each wrong option. Option lengths are comparable.

options.why: Adds the work done by friction to the kinetic energy instead of subtracting it.
The work done by friction is $-\mu mgd$, so $\tfrac12mv^2=\tfrac12mv_0^2-\mu mgd$ and $v=\sqrt{v_0^2-2\mu gd}$.
Uses the work done by friction without the factor of the acceleration due to gravity.
Subtracts the loss of speed from the initial speed without squaring, as if friction removed a speed instead of an energy.

payload.stem: A projectile is launched from level ground with a speed $v_0$ at an angle $\theta$ above the horizontal. Air resistance is negligible. Which of the following is the horizontal distance that the projectile travels before it returns to the ground?

options.why: The time of flight is $2v_0\sin\theta/g$ and the horizontal speed is $v_0\cos\theta$, so the range is $\dfrac{2v_0^2\sin\theta\cos\theta}{g}=\dfrac{v_0^2\sin2\theta}{g}$.
Divides by $2g$, which is the expression for the maximum height.
Uses the sine of the angle instead of the sine of twice the angle.
Leaves out the square of the speed.

options.text: The friction force is greater on the smaller face, $11.8\text{ N}$, because the same weight acts on a smaller area.
options.why: Confuses the pressure on the surface with the friction force; the force does not depend on the area.

payload.stem: A wooden block of mass $4\text{ kg}$ has a face of area $0.01\text{ m}^2$ and a larger face of area $0.03\text{ m}^2$. The block is pulled at constant speed along a level wooden board, first on the smaller face and then on the larger face. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the wood surfaces is $0.4$ in both cases. Which statement about the friction force is correct and best justified?

options.text: The friction force is greater on the larger face, $47\text{ N}$, because a larger area of contact gives more friction.
options.why: Assumes that the friction force is proportional to the contact area, but the model $f=\mu N$ does not include the area.

options.text: The friction force is $5.23\text{ N}$ on the larger face, because the weight is spread over a larger area.
options.why: Divides the weight by the area, but the friction force is $\mu N$ and the normal force is the same.

options.text: The friction force is greater on the smaller face, $47\text{ N}$, because the same weight acts on a smaller area.
options.why: Confuses the pressure on the surface with the friction force; the force does not depend on the area.

options.text: The friction force is $15.7\text{ N}$ in both cases, because the kinetic friction force is $\mu N$ and the normal force is the same, so the contact area does not matter.
options.why: $f=\mu N=\mu mg=15.7\text{ N}$ for either face, since $N=mg$ does not change.
